record.paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
record.original_question: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. Under which conditions on a and b does T have exactly one cycle, #C(a,b)=1? In that case, is the unique cycle necessarily the trivial cycle Ω(1), and, if G(∞)=∅ as well, does every positive integer n satisfy T^k(n)=1 for some k, so that all positive integers lie in G(1)?

A cycle of the graph associated to the map T having k vertices is a trajectory Ω for which T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω. The cardinal #Ω = Card (Ω) = k, also called the length, of Ω is in fact the smallest integer such that T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω.
G(ω ) = { n ∈ N : ∃ k ∈ N, T (k)(n) = ω } , and G(∞ ) = { n ∈ N : lim k→∞ T (k)(n) = ∞} .

3. Under which conditions on the parameters a and b, the set C(a, b ) is of cardinality #C(a, b ) = 1 ? In this case, we will see that the unique cycle in C(a, b ) is the trivial one Ω(1). If in addition G(∞ ) = ∅ , then for any integer n there exists an integer k such that T (k)(n) = 1 and we will have N = G(1).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd integers satisfying $a > -b$, and write $a + b = 2^{\nu_0}$ for some nonnegative integer $\nu_0$. Define the map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by
$$T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}, \\ (an+b)/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}. \end{cases}$$
A cycle of $T$ is a finite set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{N}$ on which some iterate $T^{(k)}$ acts as the identity, with length $k$ being the smallest such positive integer. Let $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ denote the set of all cycles of $T$ in $\mathbb{N}$. For $\omega \in \mathbb{N}$ define
$$G(\omega) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists\, k \in \mathbb{N},\ T^{(k)}(n) = \omega \}, \qquad G(\infty) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \lim_{k \to \infty} T^{(k)}(n) = \infty \}.$$
The "trivial cycle" $\Omega(1)$ is the cycle containing $1$ that arises naturally from the iteration of $T$ starting at $1$ (using $a+b = 2^{\nu_0}$, so that $T^{(\nu_0)}(1) = 1$).

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(a,b)$ under which $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$.

(b) Show that whenever $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$, the unique cycle of $T$ is $\Omega(1)$.

(c) Assuming both $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$ and $G(\infty) = \emptyset$, prove that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $T^{(k)}(n) = 1$, i.e.\ $\mathbb{N} = G(1)$.
artifact.status_search_result: The classical Syracuse/Collatz conjecture (the case $a=3,b=1$) remains open, and broader generalizations of the form $T(n)=(an+b)/2$ have been studied (e.g.\ by Matthews and others) without a general resolution; Kurtz–Simon even showed certain natural generalizations are undecidable. No source verifies a complete characterization of when $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b)=1$ or a proof that all trajectories reach $1$ under the stated hypotheses, so the problem is regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: Collatz Problem -- from Wolfram MathWorld
status_evidence.snippet: Matthews obtained results for various generalizations... Kurtz and Simon (2007) proved that a natural generalization of the Collatz problem is undecidable.
status_evidence.claim: Generalized Collatz-type maps remain unresolved in general, and some natural generalizations are undecidable.

status_evidence.title: Syracuse problem - Encyclopedia of Mathematics
status_evidence.snippet: The Syracuse / 3x+1 problem remains an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Even the classical case underlying this generalization is open.

status_evidence.title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
status_evidence.snippet: Conjectures concerning the cycle structure and trajectories of T(n)=(an+b)/2.
status_evidence.claim: The questions about uniqueness of the trivial cycle are posed as conjectures.
